Long problem 1.3: Ropes and tables (16 points)

For her 25th birthday, Alice receives an inextensible rope of length $L$ and mass $M$, distributed uniformly along its length. Initially, she feels somewhat underwhelmed by the gift, but then a spark of inspiration strikes! Remembering all the principles she learned in her mechanics class, she realises the endless possibilities this seemingly simple object holds. Excited by the challenge, Alice comes up with four distinct experiments to explore.

Each part is completely independent of the others.

Part A. Equilibrium (3.5 points)

Alice applies a force $\vec{F}$ to one end of the rope, causing $2/5$ of the rope's length to be lifted off the ground, while $3/5$ of the length remain on the ground. The rope is at equilibrum and lies in a single vertical plane. The gravitational acceleration is $\vec{g}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/swisspho-2025-3-3-fig1.png

i. (3.5 pts) Find the values of the coefficient of friction $\mu$ between the rope and the table that would allow such equilibrium to occur.

Part B. Turn around (3.5 points)

Alice puts the rope on the ground and starts pulling on it from one end going towards the other end with constant speed $v$. This time the coefficient of friction between the rope and the ground is infinite. Ignore any effects at the point where the rope curves around.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/swisspho-2025-3-3-fig2.png

i. (3.5 pts) What is the minimal force Alice needs to apply to the rope?

Part C. Slip off the table (4.5 points)

Alice leaves the rope on a table of height $h>L$ with a portion $l_0<L$ hanging on its edge. The rope is at rest at $t=0$. Assume $l_0$ is long enough, so that the rope starts slipping off the table. The coefficient of friction between the table and the rope is $\mu$. Ignore any effects at the point where the rope curves around. The gravitational acceleration is $\vec{g}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/swisspho-2025-3-3-fig3.png

i. (2.5 pts) Find the speed of the rope right as none of it is on the table anymore.

ii. (1 pt) Find the differential equation for the length of the rope hanging off the table.

iii. (1 pt) Solve the differential equation with the following Ansatz:

$$x(t)=A\cosh(\omega t)+B$$

where $A$, $B$ and $\omega$ are constants to be determined.
Hint: $\cosh(t)=\frac{1}{2}\left(\exp(t)+\exp(-t)\right)$

Part D. Hanging Masses (4.5 points)

Alice takes a smaller table and attaches two masses $m$ on each end of the rope. The left mass can only move up and down, while the right mass can move both up and down and right and left. At $t=0$, the system is at rest, such that $\theta=\varepsilon\ll 1$.

Ignore any effects at the point where the rope curves around, neglect the friction between the table and the rope and assume $m\gg M$. The gravitational acceleration is $\vec{g}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/swisspho-2025-3-3-fig4.png

i. (4.5 pts) Find the time averaged accelaration of the left mass. Consider $\dot{r}\approx 0$.
Hints:

- for $x\ll 1$, $\cos(x)\approx 1-\frac{1}{2}x^2$

- $\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^2(t)\mathrm{d}t=\int_0^{2\pi}\sin^2(t)\mathrm{d}t=\pi$

- In a polar coordinate system $(r,\theta)$, the acceleration can be written as

$$\vec{a}=(r\ddot{\theta}+2\dot{r}\dot{\theta})\vec{u_\theta}+(\ddot{r}-r\dot{\theta}^2)\vec{u_r}$$

where $\vec{u_\theta}$ is the unit vector in the angular coordinate and $\vec{u_r}$ is the unit vector in the radial coordinate.

Black holes are objects with a mass so large that not even light can escape their gravitational pull. In fact, nothing inside their event horizon can escape. problems.title: Reflections on an umbrella
problems.problem:
Long problem 2.1: Reflections on an umbrella (16 points)

We make some calculations about umbrellas and the water on the umbrellas. We model the umbrella as a flat, round disc with mass $M$ and radius $R$. Throughout the task, we neglect the surface tension of the water in particular.

Part A. The stationary umbrella / It's raining (3.75 points)

Firstly, we consider a raindrop falling from the sky. Raindrops consist of water (density: $\varrho$) and we assume that the raindrops are spherical. The air resistance acting on a falling raindrop as a function of velocity is $F=-\kappa v^2 A$ where $\kappa$ is a constant and $A$ is the cross-sectional area of the raindrop perpendicular to the direction of fall.

i. (1.5 pts) Determine the falling speed of the raindrop as a function of its radius $r_T$ when it hits the umbrella.

The rain is very heavy. The amount of rain in mass per unit area and time is $\dot m$.

ii. (1.25 pts) The force that must be applied to hold the umbrella is $F_{RS}$. Determine the radius of the raindrops $r_T$ as a function of the relevant variables. We assume that the weight of the water resting on the umbrella is negligible.

iii. (1 pt) Calculate the number of drops on the umbrella per unit of time as a function of $g,\dot m,\varrho,\kappa$ and any other variables used.

Part B. The spinning umbrella (10.75 points)

As the water collects on David's flat umbrella and drips down the edge, David begins to turn the umbrella at a constant angular velocity $\omega$, flinging the water away. As David (poor him!) has been walking in the rain for a long time, an equilibrium-like state has been reached. For simplified calculations, we model the friction as follows: The friction in the radial direction between the water and the umbrella is negligible, the tangential friction between the water and the umbrella is infinite. This means that all water can only move relative to the umbrella in the radial direction. Equivalently, you can imagine the water in radial grooves on the umbrella, which force the water onto a purely radial, straight path (from a co-rotating perspective).

i. (0.75 pts) Explain why David must always exert a torque on the umbrella despite the flow equilibrium and why this is compatible with the conservation of energy.

ii. (0.5 pts) Using the results, formulae, values and constants from Task A, determine the rate of water thrown away in mass per time.

iii. (2.5 pts) We consider a single drop of water that hits the umbrella at a distance $r_i$ from the centre of it. Find a simple expression for the velocity of the droplet at the edge of the umbrella in the radial direction if the droplet is not influenced by the rest of the water on the umbrella.

iv. (2 pts) We now return to the situation in the pouring rain. Refreshing practical experience has shown that the speed of a small volume of water depends exclusively on where it is located on the umbrella. In particular, the flow velocity is independent of where the water has fallen on the umbrella. Find an expression for the velocity of the water at distance $r$ from the centre of the umbrella that depends only on constants in addition to $r$.
Hint: The water consists of many drops that have come together in inelastic collisions. Hint: You may use the following identity without justification: $\int_0^a b\sqrt{a^2-b^2}\,\mathrm{d}b=\frac{a^3}{3}$.

v. (2 pts) Calculate how high the water is on the umbrella and show that the height is independent of the radius.

vi. (1 pt) Based on the result of the last subtask, calculate the mass moment of inertia of the umbrella including the water on it. Assume that the mass of the umbrella itself is evenly distributed.
Note: The mass moment of inertia of a cylinder with an axis of rotation coaxial to the axis of rotation through the centre of gravity is $J=\frac{1}{2}MR^2$.

vii. (1.5 pts) In a short period of time $\Delta t$, a certain amount of water is thrown away and a certain amount of water is added to the umbrella. Explain why this consideration can be used to determine the torque that David must exert on the umbrella in order to maintain its rotational speed and calculate it.

viii. (0.5 pts) Calculate the rotational energy of the entire umbrella including the water on it.

Part C. Water battle (1.5 points)

i. (1.5 pts) Calculate how far the water splashes from the centre of the umbrella when it is rotated at a height $h$ above the ground.

problems.title: Paramagnetic crystal
problems.problem:
Long problem 2.3: Paramagnetic crystal (16 points)

A crystal is made up of $N$ identical (but distinguishable), non-interacting magnetic particles, each possessing a magnetic moment of intensity $\mu$. These particles are placed in a uniform external magnetic field $\vec B$. Each magnetic moment can point either parallel or anti-parallel to the direction of the magnetic field. An example of a possible configuration of this crystal is illustrated in Figure 1.
The energy associated with each particle depends on its orientation: a magnetic moment aligned with the magnetic field has energy $-\mu B$, while one aligned against the field has energy $+\mu B$.
In this problem, we investigate how the macroscopic thermodynamic properties of the system emerge from the microscopic configurations of the particles.
Hint: For some tasks you may find uselful identities at the end of the problem.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/swisspho-2026-2-25-fig1.png

Part A. Energy of the system (4 points)

We first study the energy of the system. We call $N_+$ and $N_-$ the number of particles with magnetic moment aligned parallel and anti-parallel respectively to the direction of the magnetic field.

i. (1 pt) Express the total energy $E$ of the system as a function of the given variables.

ii. (2 pts) For what values of $N_+$ and $N_-$ is the absolute value of the energy of the system maximal and for what values is it minimal?

iii. (1 pt) Express $N_+$ and $N_-$ as a function of $N$ and the parameter $\epsilon=\frac{E}{N\mu B}$.

Part B. Entropy and temperature (8 points)

For a fixed value of the energy of the system $E$ there are multiple different configurations of the crystal that have this energy. In other words, there are multiple ways of arranging the particles in the crystal, such that its energy is a given value $E$. We call this number of configurations for a given value of the energy $\Omega(E)$.

i. (1 pt) What are the units of $\Omega(E)$?

ii. (2 pts) Express $\Omega(E)$ as a function of the given variables. Use your results from part A and recall that the particles are distinguishable.

iii. (2 pts) In statistical physics the entropy of an isolated system is

$$S=k_B\ln\Omega(E)$$

where $\ln$ is the natural logarithm and $k_B=1.38\times 10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J\cdot K^{-1}}$ is Boltzmann's constant. Show that the entropy of the crystal is

$$S=Nk_B H(\epsilon)\,,$$

where

$$H(x)=-\left[\frac{1-x}{2}\ln\left(\frac{1-x}{2}\right)+\frac{1+x}{2}\ln\left(\frac{1+x}{2}\right)\right].$$

Work with the assumption $N_\pm\gg 1$, under which Stirling's approximation applies: $\ln(n!)\approx n\ln(n)-n$.

iv. (2 pts) The statistical temperature $T_S$ of an isolated system with entropy $S$ is defined by

$$\frac{1}{T_S}=\frac{\mathrm{d}S}{\mathrm{d}E}.$$

Express the temperature of the crystal in terms of $\epsilon$.

v. (1 pt) Can this statistical temperature be negative? If yes, explain under what conditions and what does it physically represent.

Part C. Specific heat (3 points)

i. (1 pt) Invert your expression from task B.iv. to obtain an expression for $E$ as a function of $T_S$ and other variables.

ii. (1 pt) Express the specific heat $C$ of the system.

iii. (1 pt) How does $C$ behave as $T_S\to\infty$? Explain briefly why this result makes sense physically.

Part D. Dynamics (1 point)

We now consider the dynamics of the system and model them as follows. Every time interval $\Delta t$ there is a 50% probability that one of the particles (any of them) changes its magnetic moment.

i. (1 pt) If we let the dynamics run enough (i.e. in the limit $t\to\infty$), what will be the energy of the system? To what configuration does this correspond? Use a thermodynamic argument and the graph of the function $H(x)$ given in Figure D.1 to justify your answer.

You may find below useful identities.

- $\tanh(x)=\dfrac{e^x-e^{-x}}{e^x+e^{-x}}$ is the hyperbolic tangent.
- $\tanh'(x)=1-\tanh^2(x)$
- for $-1<x<1$,
$$\tanh\left(\frac{1}{2}\ln\left(\frac{1-x}{1+x}\right)\right)=-x$$

problems.problem:
Long problem 1.1: The pressure is on! (16 points)

In this exercise we want to talk about pressure. We derive different formulas and calculate a lot of stuff with it. To get the full points be sure to always first rearrange all equations, to solve it for the searched variable before putting in numbers!

Part A. Barometric altitude formula (6 points)

The barometric altitude formula yields an expression for the pressure at different heights. The goal of this part is to derive this formula.

i. (1.5 pts) Starting from pressure defined as force per unit area, derive the formula for the hydrostatic pressure $p=\rho g H$, where $\rho$ is the mass density of the fluid considered, $g$ is the gravitational acceleration and $H$ is the height of a column of that fluid.

ii. (1 pt) For the derivation of the barometric altitude formula we need the hydrostatic pressure in a differential formula: $\mathrm{d}p=\pm\rho g\,\mathrm{d}h$, where $\mathrm{d}h$ is the differential in altitude above sea level. Which sign ($+$ or $-$) should be used and why?

iii. (1.5 pts) For the barometric altitude formula we make a simplification by assuming constant temperature at all altitudes. Write down an expression for the density as a function of the pressure assuming an ideal gas. Relate two densities ($\rho$, $\rho_0$) to each other assuming isothermal condition and corresponding respective pressures ($p$, $p_0$).

iv. (2 pts) Use the correct differential formula from ii. and your expression from iii. to derive a differential expression with $p$ and $p_0$, where $p_0$ is a constant. Integrate both sides. Use the integral intervals $[p_0,p]$ and $[h_0,h_1]$. Write the result of the integration as $p(p_0,\rho_0,\Delta h)$, with $\Delta h=h_1-h_0$. This result is the barometric altitude formula.

Part B. How high are you? (5.5 points)

Now you want to use the barometric altitude formula to calculate your altitude.. However, you need an apparatus to measure the atmospheric pressure at your altitude. This is done with the apparatus shown in B.1. We have a transparent pipe filled with a liquid, where we first use water. On the left side (vacuum) the pipe is closed and on the right side the pipe is open to the atmosphere. Depending on the atmospheric pressure the height $h'$ of the liquid will change.

i. (1 pt) Express the height of the water $h'$ in terms of the atmospheric pressure.

ii. (1 pt) If we use mercury instead of water with $\rho_\mathrm{mercury}>\rho_\mathrm{water}$ how does the height $h'$ change? Why is it clever to use mercury instead of water based on the change in $h'$?

iii. (1 pt) You are using the structure with mercury ($\rho_\mathrm{mercury}=13.60\ \mathrm{g\cdot cm^{-3}}$) and know that at sea level the height of the column is $h'_0=760\ \mathrm{mm}$. What is the pressure of the atmosphere at sea level in units of Pascal?

iv. (1.5 pts) On a sunny weekend you go in the mountains and take your apparatus with you. At some point you take it out of your backpack and look at the height of the mercury column. You read of a value of $h'_1=54.2\ \mathrm{cm}$. How high above the sea level are you? Use $\rho_0=1.204\ \mathrm{kg\cdot m^{-3}}$ for the air at sea level.

v. (1 pt) What is the density of the air at your altitude?

and solve it for $T_1$. Use: $T_0=100\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ (at sea level), $\Delta H=40.6\ \mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}}$ and $R=8.31\ \mathrm{J\cdot mol^{-1}\cdot K^{-1}}$ to calculate the temperature $T_1$.

ii. (0.5 pts) You took some coffee cream with you. As usual, they are packaged in little plastic cups with an aluminum lid. The lid is deformable. Assume that the coffe cream was filled into the package at a height of $h^*=750\ \mathrm{m}$ above sea level and the package is sealed airtight. In which direction is the aluminum lid battered (in- or outward)? Explain why.

problems.title: The physics of cooking
problems.problem:
Long problem 1.2: The physics of cooking (16 points)

During the preparatory camp for the Physics Olympiad, volunteers spend a lot of time in the kitchen. In doing so, they notice a variety of physical phenomena, which will be examined in more detail below.

Part A. Cling film (2.5 points)

Cling film is used in the kitchen to cover food. However, the film tends to stick to itself, which makes covering difficult. The reason for this is the electrostatic charge of the film caused by unrolling it from the roll.

i. (1.5 pts) Determine the electric field near a single, flat piece of foil if it has a constant charge density $\sigma$.

ii. (1 pt) Two flat sheets of cling film with an area of $A$ are held on top of each other at distance $d$. Determine the force acting between the two sheets, assuming that $d\ll\sqrt{A}$ applies. Assume that the two layers each have a charge density of $\pm\sigma$.

Part B. The induction stove (5.5 points)

Induction stovesd are widely used in modern kitchens. The stove generates a time-varying magnetic field that is perpendicular to the hob and has the shape:

$$B(t)=B_0\sin(\omega t)\,.\qquad\text{(B.1)}$$

i. (1 pt) Describe how an induction cooktop heats a metal pan.

ii. (3.5 pts) First, consider a metal ring with radius $r$ that has a width $\mathrm{d}r$, thickness $b$ and specific resistance $\rho$. The metal ring is located in said magnetic field. Determine the heat output generated in the ring by the magnetic field, neglecting self-induction.

iii. (1 pt) Determine the total power generated in a pan with radius $R$ and thickness $b$ by the magnetic field, neglecting self-induction.

Part C. The soup (3.5 points)

For the starter, the kitchen team decides on a soup with mass $M$. This is placed in a perfectly insulated pot and heated by a heating rod with power $P$. However, some of the heat is lost: the heat transfer coefficient between the soup and the environment is $\lambda$ and acts on an area $A$. The ambient temperature is $T_0$ and the heat capacity of the soup is $c_s$.

Hint: The heat transfer coefficient has units of power per area per temperature.

i. (1 pt) Determine the equilibrium temperature of the soup.

ii. (1 pt) Now we add cream with mass $m$ and heat capacity $c_r$ to the soup. The cream is at ambient temperature $T_0$. Then we immediately remove the heating rod and put a lid on the pot so that no more heat exchange with the environment can take place. Determine the equilibrium temperature of the soup.

iii. (1.5 pts) We now want to refine the soup and add diced carrots to it, which have a density of $\rho_s$. Assuming that the temperature of the soup remains constant, determine the change in buoyancy of the diced carrots when they are heated from room temperature $T_0$ to the soup temperature $T_s$. The coefficient of linear expansion of the carrots is $\alpha$.

Part D. Washing up (4.5 points)

After eating, the dishes must be washed. To protect the wooden boards, they are washed by hand. To do this, a wooden board is held at an angle of $\alpha$ to the horizontal in the sink and rinsed with water. In this part, any friction can be neglected.

i. (0.5 pts) First, let's consider a drop of water initially resting on the board. Determine the acceleration of the drop along the board.

ii. (4 pts) In the general case, the drop has an initial velocity $v_0$ in any direction along the board. Find a function that encloses/describes the area that the drop could reach. What does this area look like? Determine the enveloping function.
An example of an enveloping function is shown in Figure D.1.

problems.title: Pipe Oscillator
problems.problem:
Long problem 1.3: Pipe Oscillator (16 points)

In this problem, we will analyze the electric field inside a charged pipe, through which a charge $q$ is moving.

Part A. Charged Pipe (8 points)

i. (2.5 pts) Consider a non-conducting circular ring of radius $s$ in the $xy$-plane centred at the origin, perpendicular to the $z$-axis. The ring carries a uniform line charge density $\lambda$. Show that the electric field at the point $P=(0,0,z)$ on the $z$-axis is given by

$$\mathbf{E}_\mathrm{ring}=\frac{\lambda}{2\varepsilon_0}\frac{zs}{(z^2+s^2)^{3/2}}\,\hat{z}\,,\qquad\text{(A.1)}$$

where $\hat{z}$ is the unit vector in $z$-direction.

ii. (3 pts) Consider a non-conducting hollow cylinder (open at both ends) of radius $r$ and length $2L$ whose axis coincides with the $z$-axis and whose midpoint lies at the origin. The cylinder carries a uniform surface charge density $\sigma$.
Show that the electric field at a point on the $z$-axis with $|z|\le L$ takes the form

$$\mathbf{E}_\mathrm{cyl}=\alpha\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{r^2+(L-z)^2}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{r^2+(L+z)^2}}\right)\hat{z}\,,\qquad\text{(A.2)}$$

where $\alpha$ is a constant to be determined.
Hint: $\displaystyle\int\frac{x}{(x^2+c^2)^{3/2}}\,\mathrm{d}x=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+c^2}}+C$.

iii. (2.5 pts) Now consider a non-conducting disk of radius R lying in the $xy$-plane, centered at the origin. The disc carries a uniform surface charge density $\sigma'$.
Determine a vectorial expression for the electric field of the disc at a point $P=(0,0,z)$ on the $z$-axis.
Hint: $\displaystyle\int\frac{x}{(x^2+c^2)^{3/2}}\,\mathrm{d}x=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+c^2}}+C$.

Part B. Approximations (3 points)

i. (2 pts) In the following part we are especially interested in the electric field deep inside the cylinder, that is for $|z|\ll L$. Linearise your result from the second part around $z=0$ to the form $E=kz+b$.

ii. (1 pt) Let us next consider points close to the disc, such that $R\gg|z|$. For $z>0$, find the value of $A$ in the zeroth order expression $\mathbf{E}_\mathrm{disc}\approx A\sigma'\hat{z}$.

Part C. Let it Oscillate! (5 points)

The elements analysed before are now put together. A cylinder of radius $r$, length $2L$ and uniform surface charge density $\sigma$ is centred at the origin. Two discs both of radius $R$ are placed at $z_1=-d$ and at $z_2=d$ respectively, with $d>L$. The left and right discs carry a uniform surface charge density $\sigma'$ and $-\sigma'$, respectively. Both discs are now made out of conducting material, but assume that the dimensions of the problem are such that their surface charge densities can still be considered uniform. In particular this means that $R$ is large.
A particle of mass $m$ and charge $q<0$ constrained to move on the $z$-axis is placed at the origin of the $z$-axis. Assume that $R\gg d$ and that $\sigma'(t)=\sigma_0'\cos\omega t$ for some angular frequency $\omega$ low enough such that the quasi-static approximation still holds (i.e you can use the formulas derived above). Also assume that throughout its motion, the position $z$ of the particle satisfies $|z|\ll L$.
The setup is illustrated in figure C.1.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/swisspho-2026-3-3-fig1.png

i. (4 pts) Write the linearized equation of motion of the particle in terms of $A$, $k$ and other needed quantities. Also provide an expression for the angular frequency $\omega_0$ of free oscillations of the charged particle.

ii. (1 pt) Explain what happens when $\omega\approx\omega_0$. Are your equations still valid in this case?

problems.problem:
Short question 4.6: Space-time (4 points)

Albert Einstein's theory of special relativity is based on the fundamental postulate that nothing can travel faster than the speed of light. In this exercise, we want to demonstrate the invariance of the space-time interval using the speed of light.

Part A. The definition (1.75 points)

First, let's define the terms we will be using.

i. (0.5 pts) The space-time interval plays a central role in special relativity. Write the equation for the space-time interval $(\Delta s)^2$ between two events $s$ and $s'$.
Note: The spacetime interval is the difference between the squares of the temporal and spatial distances between the two events.

ii. (1.25 pts) Define the Lorentz transformation in all 4 space-time components for a boost with velocity $v$ in the $y$-direction. Note that a boost with velocity $\vec{v}$ is a change to a reference system moving at velocity $\vec{v}$ with respect to the current system.
Note: Use the Lorentz factor $\gamma=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\beta^2}}$, with $\beta=\frac{v}{c}$.

Part B. Speed of light (2.25 points)

Now let's use the definitions in the previous sub-task to perform calculations. Consider switching on a lamp at space-time point $(0,0,0,0)$. Since the light propagates in all direction with the speed of light it will form a sphere. In a reference frame where the lamp is moving with constant velocity, the emitted light also propagates in all directions with the speed of light (this is one of the postulates of special relativity). In the following subtasks we will demonstrate that a space-time interval is invariant under a Lorentz transformation.

i. (0.75 pts) Consider the sphere of the light from the lamp spreading out in all spatial dimensions in a stationary system with respect to the lamp. Look at the two events at $s_1=(0,0,0,0)$ and $s_2=(t,x,y,z)$, when the light first reaches the point $(x,y,z)$, and calculate its space-time interval. Show that the space-time interval vanishes.

ii. (1.5 pts) Consider the two events from B.i. in a moving reference frame moving with velocity $v$ in $y$-direction with respect to the original one. Use the Lorentz transformation obtained in part A ii. to transform the coordinates of these events to the moving reference frame. Show that their space-time interval vanishes also in the moving frame.
